title: David Hackett Fischer’s “Albion’s Seed”
author: https://hedgehogreview.com/contributors/michael-lind
text:
In the second installment of the Federalist Papers, John Jay declared that “Providence has been pleased to give this one connected country to one united people—a people descended from the same ancestors, speaking the same language, professing the same religion, attached to the same principles of government, very similar in their manners and customs.” Jay was only half right. True, the majority of white Americans at the time of the War of Independence and the adoption of the federal Constitution were of British descent, Protestant, and “similar in their manners and customs” compared to French Canadians or Latin Americans or Afro-Caribbean people. But within the group of American settlers from the British Isles were differences in British regional origins, kinds of Protestantism, and “manners and customs” in each region of the United States. 

That is the thesis of the historian David Hackett Fischer in Albion’s Seed: Four British Folkways in America, published in 1989. In this widely reviewed and influential study, Fischer argued that the United States has been profoundly shaped by the enduring legacies of four streams of emigration from the British Isles during the Colonial period. The Puritan migration up to 1630 planted the seeds of what later became the culture of New England, which in the nineteenth century spread to the upper Midwest and the Pacific Coast. A second wave of aristocratic Anglican “Cavaliers” from the south of England occurred between the 1640s and the 1670s, as many Royalists left Britain during the English Civil War and Cromwell’s Puritan dictatorship (1642–1651) for Virginia and the surrounding area. The third wave, from the 1670s to the 1710s, brought egalitarian, pacifist Quakers from the North Midlands of England to the Delaware Valley. The fourth and final wave of British emigration before American independence was that of the rowdy and clannish Scots-Irish, or “borderers,” from Ulster, the Scottish Lowlands, and northern England, between 1717 and 1775. “Most broad areas of consensus in American life have grown from values that these cultures shared in common,” Fischer concluded. “Many major conflicts in American history have developed primarily from their differences.” 

While the depth of historical detail and sociological research that informed Albion’s Seed was unprecedented, Fischer’s emphasis on cultural genealogy as the key to understanding cultural geography in the United States was a revival of a scholarly tradition that had been eclipsed in the twentieth century. Thomas Jefferson, for example, shared with eighteenth-century Whigs the belief that the Anglo-Saxons and related Teutonic tribes who invaded the British Isles in the Dark Ages had brought the “germ,” or seed, of liberty from the forests of Germany. Tragically, the free constitution of Alfred the Great’s Anglo-Saxon England had been snuffed out in 1066 by William the Conqueror, who imposed the “Norman yoke” of feudalism and despotic monarchy on Britain. Jefferson was unsuccessful when he proposed that one side of the Great Seal of the United States portray “Hengist and Horsa, the Saxon chiefs from whom we claim the honor of being descended, and whose political principles and form of government we have assumed.” But he succeeded in persuading the University of Virginia to adopt the first college-level course in Anglo-Saxon, the supposed language of liberty and democracy.

In English Traits (1856), Ralph Waldo Emerson declared that Anglo-Saxons were responsible for modern progress and were superior to the lowly Celtic race (take that, Boston Irish immigrants!). As odd as it seems today, many of the same New Englanders who, like Emerson, took pride in their real or imagined Teutonic ancestry were reformists who supported causes like the abolition of slavery and the temperance movement.

In contrast, many in the antebellum Southern elite identified with the aristocratic Normans rather than with the humble Saxons and identified the two groups with the Royalists and Roundheads, respectively, of the English Civil War. The Southern gentry could be as disdainful of their own Celts, the Protestant Scots-Irish of Appalachia and the Ozarks, as the Yankees were of Irish Catholic immigrants in the North. In 1780, the English-born American General Charles Lee complained to his fellow Virginian James Monroe about the influence of the Scots-Irish in state politics: “We have now neither a monarchy, Aristocracy, nor Democracy…it is rather a Mac-ocracy, by which I mean that a Banditti of low Scotch-Irish who are either themselves imported servants or the immediate descendants of imported servants are the Lords Paramount.”

The germ theory of Anglo-American liberty was reinforced around the turn of the twentieth century by German-trained American political scientists like Columbia’s John William Burgess. World War I provoked a crisis for the Teutonist interpretation of American history, which before 1914 viewed the three Protestant powers—the United States, the United Kingdom, and Bismarckian Germany—as the three most progressive nations of modern times. The definition of World War I as a battle of democracy versus autocracy led to the replacement of the militarist, autocratic Germans by the democratic French as ideological allies of America and Britain. Following World War I, the notion that the United States was the heir of a de-ethnicized “Western civilization,” whose line of descent led from ancient Greek democracy via the eighteenth-century Enlightenment to a modern democratic nation-state, came to dominate American scholarship and public discourse.

In the decades following World War I, the germ theory was replaced by progressive historians, such as Charles Beard, who emphasized conflict among economic interest groups. And after 1945 came the “consensus theory” of the Cold War era, which held that American politics had always rested on the shared philosophy of Lockean liberalism. 

Albion’s Seed was thus an implicit rebuke to nearly a century of American historical scholarship. Its importance was immediately recognized by other prominent American historians. Gordon Wood described Albion’s Seed as a “revisionist blockbuster,” while Edmund S. Morgan declared that it would inspire “the research of many other historians,” and Eric S. Foner observed “how successful Fischer is in casting colonial America in a new light.”

Yet Fischer’s emphasis on the importance of enduring regional subcultures in the United States had precedents in the work of other scholars. In American Federalism: A View From the States (1966), Daniel J. Elazar argued for three distinct regional political subcultures—moralistic (from New England through the upper North to the West Coast), traditionalistic (the South and Southwest), and individualistic (the Midwest). 

These happened to overlap with the linguist Hans Kurath’s mapping of dialects of the United States, which tended to follow the westward migration of different groups of British settlers from the Eastern seaboard. The geographer Donald W. Meinig provided an in-depth analysis of American regional histories in his four-volume series The Shaping of America, published between 1986 and 2004. Fischer’s significance is that the sheer detail of his 946-page tome at once synthesized these similar approaches and forced American historians to acknowledge them.

Unfortunately, Fischer failed to found a new academic school of American history. His admirers are mostly found among political journalists and popular historians like Colin Woodard, author of American Nations: A History of the Eleven Rival Regional Cultures of North America (2011). 

In American university history departments, Fischer and like-minded scholars were eclipsed between the 1990s and the present by a new identity-politics school, which holds that American history has revolved around white supremacy and the oppression of “people of color” (a catchall term for quite different groups, including Native Americans, black Americans, Hispanic Americans, and Asian Americans). This approach became mainstream with the publication, in theNew York Times Magazine in 2019, just before the 2020 height of the Black Lives Matter protests, of a collection of writing conceived by the journalist Nikole Hannah-Jones that became the 2021 book The 1619 Project: A New Origin Story. Notwithstanding critiques of the factual errors in the essays and the book, the New York Times and the Pulitzer Center promoted curricula based on the book to public schools, in a heavy-handed attempt to impose a new quasi-official history on the United States. The claim that conventional American history before 2019 downplayed the role of racism and slavery and the Civil War and the civil rights revolution was a libel on American educators, while the assertion that since 1619 black-white relations have eclipsed all intra-white regional, religious, and economic conflicts in political significance was obviously false. 

The long-delayed backlash from the right against leftist identity politics in education and the media arrived with the second Trump administration and its assaults on DEI and rewriting of what it considered “woke” history in American museums and national monuments. The backlash included an outbreak of more or less overt white nationalism among far-right online influencers. Some claimed that “real” Americans are “Heritage Americans,” defined as Anglo-American, Protestant, and descended from Colonial-era British settlers. Ironically, right-wing Heritage Americanism, like left-wing identity politics, erases the very regional and subcultural distinctions among white Americans of British descent highlighted by Fischer. Nineteenth-century Yankees who thought of themselves as Anglo-Saxons and nineteenth-century Southerners who claimed to be descendants of Norman barons would have been surprised to learn they were part of one big happy Heritage American family.

It might be thought that waves of emigration from Catholic Ireland and Continental Europe, and more recently from Latin America, Asia, and other parts of the world, would have eroded the regional cultures identified by Fischer. Indeed, that seems to have happened in the Mid-Atlantic area between Baltimore and New York, where few traces of the Quaker “hearth culture” survive, other than a certain informality.

In other regions, however, the assimilation of immigrants tends to follow what the cultural geographer Wilbur Zelinsky defined in his 1973 book, The Cultural Geography of the United States, as the Doctrine of First Effective Settlement: “The dominant culture of a given nation is determined by the characteristics of the first group of settlers who came to an empty territory regardless of how small the initial band of settlers might have been.” Outnumbered by the majority in an area, later immigrants, unless they belong to numerous diasporas, tend to assimilate to the folkways and values of the local majority. This explains why Southern Jews, outside of Florida, a retirement haven for Northern Jews, tend to be more conservative than Northern Jews.

For their part, despite some subcultural differences, black Americans of Southern descent have more in common with white Americans, in dialect, religion, and cuisine, than either group does with Americans in other regions. In Black Rednecks and White Liberals (2005), the black conservative scholar Thomas Sowell argued that stereotypically black “ghetto” culture of transplanted black Southerners in the North, with shootings often motivated by “disrespect,” is a version of the folk culture of poor white Southern “rednecks” and “crackers.” Another possible source is the Cavalier culture of slave owners in the coastal plantation South, with their penchant for duels of honor. Americans of Southern descent, of both races, have higher rates of violence than other Americans, including black immigrants from the Caribbean. 

The persistence of Fischer’s regional cultures on American national politics is manifest. For most of American history there has been a Northern party, shaped by New England Puritan moralism and communitarianism, based in Greater New England—variously called the Federalists, the National Republicans, the Whigs, and the Republicans—opposing a Southern and Southwestern party dominated by the heirs of the Cavaliers—Jefferson’s Republicans, the Democratic-Republicans, the Democrats, and now the Republicans (again!). The Midwest and Mountain and Plains West have often been electoral battlegrounds, and the loyalties of the Scots-Irish in greater Appalachia have sometimes been divided. 

If you look at maps of the presidential Electoral College by states, this pattern continues. The Democratic electoral heartland in 2024 included the states of New England and areas of nineteenth-century Yankee settlement in the upper Midwest and California and the rest of the West Coast. The Republican candidate, Trump, swept the South, the base of today’s Republican Party, and the Interior West, and won enough swing states in the Midwest to win the White House for a second, non-consecutive term.

But the picture is strikingly different at the county level. In 2024, rural counties in almost every state voted Republican, while populous cities, even in conservative Southern states, voted for the Democrat. In contrast, the county map of the 1924 election shows shared partisanship at city, county, and state levels in majority-Republican or majority-Democratic states, with the few exceptions being isolated ethnic minorities like German Americans and Mexican Americans in Texas, who voted for the Republicans against nativist and racist Democrats.

What seems to have happened is that since the late twentieth century former regional cultures have become detached from their original regions and incorporated into partisan, educational, and professional identities. Universities in every region, even colleges in the South, which once proudly maintained local elite traditions, have become generic and homogenized. The national academic culture everywhere reflects that of Ivy League universities such as Harvard and Yale that still bear the influence of New England Congregationalism. Corresponding to Elazar’s “moralistic” subculture, woke progressivism, in its zeal for “social justice” and post-Protestant rituals, is best understood as a secular descendant of New England Puritanism by way of nineteenth-century Boston Transcendentalism and the early-twentieth-century Northeastern Social Gospel.

While secular Puritanism has captured American universities and nonprofits, the Southern Cavalier tradition is embodied in the US military. Except for a generation following the Civil War, Southerners have been over-represented in the US military since the founding of the nation. In today’s professional military, many soldiers and officers are from military families, often Southern, leading some to warn of the rise of a military “caste” that is more conservative and more pro-war than the rest of American society in the twenty-first century. 

Even as religious belief overall declines in the United States, the fastest-growing Christian churches in America are nondenominational Protestant churches, concentrated in the South. In popular culture, country music, with its Scots-Irish origins, influenced by Southern black music, is fast-growing and the favorite of rural Americans in almost every region. NASCAR, which originated during the Prohibition era with bootleggers in Scots-Irish Appalachia, is now the leading motorsport and one of the seven most popular sports in America. Appropriately enough, President Trump, who is best described as a modern-day Jacksonian, has ordained that the two hundred fiftieth anniversary of the United States, in 2026, will be celebrated by a car race through the streets of Washington, DC.

A phantom version of the Roman Empire survived in the form of the Catholic Church, whose popes until recently were almost all Italians. In the same way, even as mass media and domestic and international migration have blurred regional differences, the folkways identified by David Hackett Fischer in Albion’s Seed have survived by being partly incorporated into the internal cultures of specific American institutions like the universities, the military, and popular culture. Far from becoming extinct in the twenty-first century United States, at least three of Fischer’s four British folkways—those of the Puritans, the Cavaliers, and the Scots-Irish borderers—have simultaneously become nationalized and institutionalized. 

Detached from their ethnic and regional origins and attached to class-based cultures, the British-American traditions Fischer identifies may endure, as nonwhite immigrants and their descendants assimilate to multiple melting pots along educational and occupational lines. Already in the US, college-educated Hispanics tend to share the liberalism of other college-educated Americans, reflecting the New England roots of today’s academic culture, while working-class Hispanics are more socially conservative, and many convert to evangelical Protestantism, with its Scots-Irish influences.

Meanwhile, the nativism of today’s “Heritage Americans” on the right is much more inclusive than that of the Anglo-Protestant nativists of a century ago, with Irish Americans and German Americans now considered “Heritage Americans.”

This is because in the twentieth century formerly distinct Anglo-Americans and other white ethnic groups merged. Rising rates of racial intermarriage today—nearly a third of new marriages for Hispanics and Asian Americans, one in five for black Americans—are rendering today’s racial and ethnic categories, and therefore contemporary nativism, obsolete. If there are any nativists in 2100, they may declare that authentic “Heritage Americans” are of British, European, Latin American, and Asian descent, excluding whatever immigrants of the time they dislike.

Paradoxically, as intermarriage increases, more and more Americans will have both recent non-European ancestors and distant white American ancestors. Thanks to intermarriage, over time growing numbers of nonwhite and mixed-race Americans will be able to claim partial descent from British settlers in the Colonial era. Americans who are mostly of Hispanic and Asian descent might be able to claim a Mayflower or a Virginia Cavalier ancestor. In an increasingly diverse America, then, at least some of Fischer’s British American hearth cultures will live on—not only in widespread folkways but also in widely shared genes.
